en: *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra*, Scroll One.
Translator’s name lost; appended to the Later Han Record.
(1) When a Bodhisattva delivers sentient beings, it is like a skillful wet-nurse raising a child, which involves four matters: first—

First, bathing them to make them clean; second, nursing them to satisfy their hunger; third, laying them to rest so they may sleep peacefully; and fourth, carrying them in and out while constantly ensuring they remain joyful.
By means of these four matters, one nurtures one's children until they attain fulfillment.
The Bodhisattva is likewise; there are four matters by which he nurtures sentient beings:

first, bathing the defilements of the mind with the True Dharma; second, satiating them with the food and drink of the sutras and teachings; third, establishing meditative concentration and samādhi at the appropriate times; and fourth, benefiting all through the four kinds of kindness, constantly causing them to rejoice.
By means of these four matters, he exhorts all beings and nurtures sentient beings so that they may attain the Supreme Way.
(2) There are two kinds of worldly knowledge that constantly act as conditions for people, causing them to incur great sin and also causing them to obtain great merit.
What are the two types of spiritual friends?
First, the evil spiritual friend; second, the virtuous spiritual friend.

For example, it is like a master thief who commits rebellious acts against his sovereign and father, killing them and bringing chaos to the world. All sentient beings suffer from the calamities of his poison without exception; associating with such a person causes others to incur great sin.

Just as the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni resolved his mind to seek the Way to rescue and protect sentient beings, employing the four immeasurables and the four debts of gratitude to embrace and guard all, there is none throughout the three realms and five paths who does not receive his deliverance!
What is called a "good friend" (kalyāṇamitra) is one who associates with whom one gains great merit.
(3) Once, in South India, there was a country named Sihakṣa, situated upon an island in the sea; its city measured more than eighty thousand li in length and breadth.

At that time, there was an old woman from another country named Āluṅ who, having encountered the calamities of a period of upheaval, had wandered to this country. Being solitary and having no place to go, she lived by begging and went to the house of the elder, wishing to seek shelter.
At that time, the elder’s wife saw her and greeted the old woman; the old woman then fully explained her circumstances of poverty and distress.
The elder was moved with compassion for her and said to the old woman, "You may stay in my house, and I shall provide you with all necessary support."

The old woman said joyfully, "I have nothing with which to repay you in a grand manner; I shall serve as your humble handmaid, and I shall not dare to shrink from the toil of whatever tasks you assign."
He then stopped and stood still, his heart filled with both sorrow and joy:

"In the past, I provided for the assembly of monks according to their every wish; today, I have suddenly fallen into such dire straits that my intention to give cannot be fulfilled, and I am moved by deep personal grief."
After first prostrating himself before the practitioner and completing his inquiries, he asked:
"I wonder whether the midday meal has been prepared for the Sangha?
The practitioner replied:
"I entered the city this morning to beg for alms but obtained nothing; therefore, I have returned to where I stayed.
The old woman then thought to herself:
"I wish to provide food for the assembly of monks, yet I myself possess nothing at all."
He said to the various practitioners, "I shall now enter the city to observe; if provisions can be prepared, I will return and inform you;
if not, I shall likewise let you know the news."
Thereupon the assembly gave their consent, and each person moved on to dwell beneath a tree.
Then the old woman returned to her home and informed the householder’s wife that she should spend several thousand coins, saying:
"Although I am currently serving here as a laborer, I wish to sell myself into lifelong slavery; may a formal contract be established?"
The householder’s wife asked, "You rely on me for food and clothing while staying here; why have you suddenly spent money? What have you done with it?"
The old woman replied, "I have an urgent need for it; I cannot afford to give it up.
Thereupon, the elder’s wife gave her the money and said:
"To keep this for my own use, I might return it later when the time is right; what need have I for a receipt?
Having received the money, the old woman went to those among her acquaintances with whom she had long been familiar and informed them of the situation in detail:
"I shall give the money to each person so that they may provide offerings for sixty households."
In a short while, she had finished preparing it and brought it to the practitioner,
saying, "I originally thought there was no real certainty [in your practice],
yet upon reaching the city, you have become like this. They all marveled that her diligence was beyond their expectations and asked the old woman:
“Where do you reside?
Morning after morning, I have gone on my alms-round without a village left unvisited; why have we not encountered one another at all?
The old woman then related the beginning and end of the matter in full detail.
"I am a native of a certain kingdom, and my family has long been devoted to the Buddha and made offerings to the Sangha.

Having encountered the chaos and turmoil of the world, we were driven into exile until we arrived here. Our household wealth was completely exhausted and I remained all alone; I have taken refuge with the family of a great elder of this country, serving as his attendant and relying on him for food and clothing. I am destitute, having entrusted my life to him without possessing even a single coin."
Seeing the practitioner, his heart was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy; harboring a certain thought, he lamented that his compassionate vow had not yet been fulfilled.
He said to his wife:
"I shall sell myself to seek a small amount of money, wishing to provide food for the assembly of monks."
“Out of compassionate grace and pity, you have allowed my humble sincerity to be fulfilled!
The practitioner sighed and said,
“Truly, this may be called the ultimate fulfillment of faith and giving!”
They all said to one another, "We too have been seeking alms with bodies composed of the five aggregates; today’s food is indeed human flesh. We ought each to resolve to repay this act of giving."

The multitude united their hearts to establish the eightfold application of mindfulness (*aṣṭa-smṛtyupasthāna*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); through the resonance of their perfected refinement, they immediately attained transcendent absorption (*samādhi*). Their supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) and majestic spiritual authority shook the surrounding realm, causing the trees to bend their branches as if prostrating in worship.
The practitioners witnessed this and praised the donor.
The king was struck with awe and wonder at the reason for such an occurrence; he summoned his ministers to deliberate together:
"Considering the origin of this auspicious omen, by what cause has it been brought about?"

The ministers went out in the four directions to investigate the cause, and they saw that outside the city gates a great multitude of people had gathered; donors were present in abundance, and they all celebrated and relied upon one another.
He immediately entered and informed the king, who said, "This is exactly what I intended; summon him here at once!
The minister returned and proclaimed the king's command.
The old woman, trembling with fear at the prospect of some misfortune, replied to the minister:
"My person is bound to the wife of the elder; I have no freedom.
The minister returned and reported these words to the king, who said:
"Summon her as well. Thereupon, having heard the king's command, the householder’s wife immediately went with the old woman to the king's presence.
The king asked for their purpose, and the old woman related the matter from beginning to end, saying to the king: [text continues]

The king said, "I am the sovereign of a nation, possessing great wealth and power; yet I did not know how to revere the Three Honored Ones or make offerings to the Daoists, whereas this old mother has been able to move them so profoundly!"
The King said, "This mother is my teacher. He ushered her into the palace,
bathed her with fragrant water, and seated her upon the teacher's throne.
The palace attendants and court ladies numbered twenty thousand; the King himself received the precepts and became an upāsaka, while the elderly women and court ladies became upāsikās.
All the people of the country universally resolved to attain the Way.
(4) Once, a practitioner of the Way was studying the Path in the mountains.

The mountains were infested with many venomous snakes (*āśīviṣa*). Fearing them, the practitioner took refuge beneath a tree, where he set up a high platform and sat in meditation, contemplating concentration;
however, he could not control himself and fell into a deep, troubled sleep.

The celestial being laughed in the air; [the monk] woke up, then fell back asleep. Not understanding why the celestial being had employed such a skillful means, he wished to frighten him so that he would not sleep excessively.
At night, a celestial being said, "Alas, O practitioner! A venomous snake has come!
The practitioner was greatly terrified; he immediately lit a lamp and searched everywhere, but could not see it.
The devas came repeatedly and without ceasing, so the practitioner became even more resentful and said:
"Why do these devas commit double-tongued speech?
Seeing nothing at all, how can they claim that every word is like a venomous serpent?"
The celestial being said to the practitioner:
"Why do you not observe the internal venomous snakes for yourself?
Within your body there are four snakes that have not been removed; how can you seek them further from the outside?"
Upon hearing the words of the deva, the practitioner immediately reflected within himself:

"Observing my own body through its internal organs, I realize that the four great elements have been submerged by the five aggregates and the six sense-fields; from countless kalpas until now, I have not yet attained liberation."
He immediately realized the Four Noble Truths—that they are suffering, empty, and not-self.
Before dawn, his outflows were exhausted and his mind was liberated; he became fully endowed with the six supernormal powers and attained arhatship.
(5) Once there was King Aśoka, who established one thousand two hundred stupas and monasteries within his realm. Later, he fell ill and became severely distressed.
A certain śramaṇa went to visit the king; when they met, the king was so overcome with grief that he could not control himself.
The practitioner said, "The meritorious deeds the King has performed throughout your life are beyond counting; you should broaden your mind and harbor no resentment!"
The king said: "Even if death were to arrive, I could have no cause for regret. The reason I am grieved is this:

previously, for the sake of twelve hundred monasteries, I had each woven twelve hundred golden-threaded banners and canopies, intending to hang the banners myself and scatter flowers within them. Now that the materials for all these monasteries have finally been prepared, I have fallen gravely ill; fearing I shall not fulfill my original vow, it is for this reason alone that I lament!"
The practitioner said to the king, “Very well!
With palms joined and a single-minded focus, he caused the king to see all the stupas within the entire realm.
The practitioner of the Way immediately manifested his supernormal powers, and at that moment, the twelve hundred stupas all appeared before the king.

Seeing this, he was filled with great joy; his illness was instantly cured. He took golden banners and golden flowers and hung them upon the various shrines; the stupas and temples tilted and rose as they were guided by the king’s hand.

The king attained his original vow-body and his illness was healed; he immediately resolved upon the Great Mind, extending his life for twenty-five years, and subsequently performed meritorious deeds until he reached the stage of non-retrogression.

6. (Sixth) Formerly, there was King Aśoka, who was installed in the position of governance; twenty-eight myriad *li* were all under his dominion. Even the terrestrial nāgas, yakṣas, and others offered tribute as subjects and envoys; there were none who did not submit.

There was only one dragon king who resided in a pond within the northern border measuring over three hundred li in width; having obtained one portion of the Buddha’s relics, he made offerings to them day and night, alone refusing to submit to King Aśoka.
The king immediately raised his fourfold army and went to the edge of the lake, but the dragon did not emerge to respond.
The dragon possessed majestic spiritual power, and the king was likewise unable to advance.
Thus he went three times, yet he could not capture the dragon.
"The reason his majestic spiritual power is so superior is that his merit surpasses mine!
I shall now perform great meritorious deeds to make offerings to the Triple Gem; by doing so, I will surely attain my goal without doubt!"
Thereupon, he constructed stūpas and monasteries and extensively invited the Saṃgha, doing so repeatedly without ceasing.

Desiring to test his own merit, he fashioned a golden dragon and a figure of a king, placing them on the two ends of a scale to weigh their relative lightness and heaviness. He weighed both images together as they performed meritorious deeds; at first, the dragon was heavy and the king was light.
Later, when he weighed them again, the scale was perfectly balanced.
He further performed meritorious deeds; subsequently, King Aśoka’s weight increased daily while the Dragon King’s weight decreased daily.

Knowing that his merit was increasing day by day, the king raised an army to go and subdue him. Before they had even reached the halfway point, the dragon king, along with his followers both great and small, came out to welcome him and submitted. The portion of the Buddha’s relics he had obtained, one part, he offered to King Aśoka, who then rebuilt stūpas and monasteries and extensively propagated the Buddha-dharma.

(7) Once, one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was King Aśoka, who cherished the Buddha-dharma. Within his kingdom there were twenty thousand bhikṣus, whom the king constantly provided with offerings.
The ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders gave rise to feelings of jealousy and plotted to destroy the Buddha-dharma; they gathered together and deliberated on a stratagem.
Among them was one man skilled in illusion who said to the crowd:
"I wish to perform an illusion by transforming myself into the form of an evil ghost to seek out the śramaṇas; upon hearing this, they will surely disperse and perish."
"You should know that they are not equal; they will surely come to return to our Way!
The deity worshipped by the heterodox sect was named Maheśvara, who had one head, four faces, eight eyes, and eight arms; he was the most fearsome among all the ghosts.

The brahmin immediately assumed this form and, leading more than two hundred hideous spirits, traveled majestically through the kingdom, gradually advancing until he reached the gate of the royal palace.
The men and women of the entire kingdom were without exception struck with terror. When the king went out to meet him, he beheld the Great Terrifying Ghost; bowing his head in prostration, he asked:
"I wonder what command the Great Deity desires?"
The ghost said to the king,
"I wish to eat a person.
The king said:
"That cannot be! The ghost said, "If Your Majesty cherishes your people,
then let those in the kingdom who are of no benefit to the king be handed over to me for consumption."
The king said, "There is none! The ghost said:
"These śramaṇas neither farm nor serve in the military, nor do they pay tribute to the king; since they are of no benefit, hand them over to me to devour."
The king’s heart was unhappy, yet having no other recourse, he dispatched a messenger to Jetavana to convey the news.
Among the twenty thousand bhikṣus was a most junior śrāmaṇera, thirteen years of age, named Sundara, who addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall go and respond to this!”
He immediately granted permission.
The śrāmaṇera went outside and said to the karmadāna, "If there is any brahmin who enters the Jeta Grove, shave his head together with the others; do not let him escape."
He then went to where the spirits were and said to them:
"I know that you have come wishing to devour us; as we are the youngest among the monks, we have come first to arrange the order for you. The other bhikṣus will follow in due succession."
The śrāmaṇera spoke again:
"I have not yet received food since morning; let you all feed me so that I may be fully satiated, and then I shall eat you.
The spirit granted his request.
At that time, there were also more than twenty thousand followers of the ghost-ascetics (bhūta-brāhmaṇas), for whom the king was preparing a great feast.
The śrāmaṇera then took the food for those twenty thousand people, placed it all into his mouth, and by means of his supernormal power (ṛddhi), flew to the Jetavana Monastery.
Not yet being satiated, he again took twenty thousand Brahmins and swallowed them, likewise using his supernormal powers to send them back into the Jeta Grove.
At that time, the illusory Brahmin fled in great terror; he was restored to his human form, prostrated himself to apologize for his transgression, and requested to become a disciple.
The bhikṣus shaved the heads of all the brahmins and preached the Dharma to them, whereby they all attained arhatship.
Among the people of the entire kingdom, there was none who did not rejoice, obtain merit, and attain liberation.
King reflected and said:
"If even a single young śrāmaṇera can move me in such a way, what might not be found within the ocean of the Mahāyāna?
I shall now resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
From that time forth, the Buddha-dharma flourished and has not ceased to this day.
(8) In the past, there was a king who delighted in eating human flesh. He commanded his cooks, saying:
"You must travel by night in secret to capture people and bring them here for my kitchen."
He took this to be the constant rule.
Later, when his ministers all became aware of this, they collectively expelled him beyond the borders and sought out another virtuous and worthy man to serve as king.

Thus, after thirteen years, the man-eating king grew two wings upon his body; he traveled about devouring people regardless of distance, whether near or far. In the mountains, he approached the tree deity and requested a blessing, saying:
"I shall seize a king and five hundred men as an offering to the mountain tree deity, so that I may return to my kingdom and become its king once more."
Thereupon, he flew through the air to seize them, capturing four hundred and ninety-nine people and bringing them to a mountain valley where he sealed the opening with stones.

At that time, the king, accompanied by his harem, went to a bathing pool to play. As he was just leaving the palace gate, he encountered a practitioner who spoke a verse seeking alms; the king immediately granted his request, promising to bestow gold and silver upon his return to the palace.
At that time, as the king entered the pool intending to bathe, a man-eater flew down from the sky, seized the king, and departed back to the mountains.
Upon seeing the man-eater, the king felt neither fear nor terror, his countenance remaining unchanged.

The Man-eating King said, "I originally captured five hundred men to offer as a sacrifice to the gods; there were already four hundred and ninety-nine, and now that I have obtained you, one more, the number is complete. I shall kill you to sacrifice to the gods."
"You know this; why then do you not feel dread?
The king replied, "In human life there is death, in things accomplished there is decay, and in meeting there is separation; since these are the natural divisions of existence, I dare not grieve."

"When I left the palace this morning, I encountered a Daoist on the road who recited a verse for me; at that time, I promised to bestow goods upon him, yet I have not yet been able to give them. This is the cause of my regret!"
"Now, as Your Majesty is magnanimous and forgiving, if you complete your acts of giving within a few days and return, you shall not violate your solemn vow!
He immediately granted him leave to depart and addressed him, saying:
"I grant you a period of seven days; if you do not return, it will not be difficult for me to go and fetch you myself!"

The king immediately returned to the palace in the capital; everyone, both inside and outside the court, was filled with joy. He opened the treasuries to bestow gifts upon those far and near, installed the crown prince as king, and after consoling the common people, he took his leave and departed.
The Man-eating King saw him approaching from afar and thought to himself:
"Could this not be a strange person?
Having returned to life from death, he has come back here."

He then asked: "Body and life are what the world prizes and cherishes; yet you have renounced that which you hold dear, a feat difficult for the world to achieve. I wonder, what is the resolve and aspiration by which you maintain your purpose?"
"I pray that you will explain its meaning. He then said:
"My compassionate giving is based on a sincere and truthful vow: I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and deliver all beings throughout the ten directions."
The king asked, "What is the meaning of seeking the Buddha? What are its practices?
Thereupon, [the teacher] explained at length the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, the four immeasurables, and the six perfections.

His mind opened and became serene; he received the five precepts and became a lay follower (*upāsaka*). He released four hundred and ninety-nine people, each ordering them to return to their own countries.

The various kings followed this later king to his country; moved by his sincere oath and having been spared from death, they each refused to return to their native lands and subsequently settled in this country.

For each of these kings, a premier residence was established, exquisitely carved and adorned with intricate ornamentation, magnificent and orderly; their food, drink, clothing, and utensils were provided such that they were no different from those of the king.
People coming from the four directions asked,
"Why is it that this city is like Rājagṛha throughout the entire kingdom?
The multitude answered:
"All these are the dwellings of kings!
Thus his name became widely renowned,
and from that time forward, it was called the City of Rājagṛha (the King’s Dwelling).
After the Buddha had attained the Way, he himself recounted the beginning and end of these events:

"The King who established the faith was I myself; the man-eating king was Aṅgulimāla. When I returned to Rājagṛha to preach the Dharma, those whom I saved were immeasurable—all of them were people with whom I shared karmic conditions during our past lives as kings!"
When the Buddha had spoken these words, all were filled with joy; they obtained merit and attained deliverance in numbers beyond calculation.
(9) Formerly, on the Snowy Mountains, there was a king of white elephants who possessed six tusks and fathered twenty thousand elephants.
The Elephant King had two consorts, one elder and one younger; whenever he went out for recreation, they attended him on his left and right.
Once, as the King was traveling for pleasure, he passed a great tree with lush and beautiful blossoms, which he desired to pluck to adorn the bodies of his two consorts.

She twisted the branches of the *nāgapuṣpa* tree to shake it, and the wind blew the flowers so that they fell only upon the Senior Queen; the Junior Queen, being downwind, received no flowers. She thought the King was partial and conceived a poisonous heart within her.
Later, a golden thousand-petaled lotus grew in the king’s pond; seeing it, the young elephant took it and presented it to the king. The king gave it to his chief queen, who placed it upon her head.
Thereupon, the junior queen became even more envious and enraged, and she conceived a desire to harm the king.

In the Snowy Mountains there were many practitioners of the Way. Thereupon, the junior consort gathered beautiful fruits and constantly made offerings to a hundred pratyekabuddhas. Later, standing on a precipitous part of the mountain, she made this vow:

"By the merit and retribution of these offerings to the pratyekabuddhas, may I be reborn among humans with noble power and the ability to remember my past lives, so that I may kill this elephant king."
He immediately cast his body down from the mountain and died.
His spirit was reborn among humans as the daughter of an elder; she was possessed of brilliant wisdom, far-reaching insight, and was peerless in her exquisite beauty.
When the girl had grown up, the king took her as his consort and held her in great affection.
The consort thought to herself:
"Now I have truly avenged my old grudge!"
She then smeared her face with yellow *kīraṇa* (yellowness) and lay prostrate, feigning illness.
When the king entered to inquire after her, she replied, "Last night I dreamed of an elephant with six tusks; I wish to obtain those tusks to fashion hairpins from them."
"If Your Majesty does not obtain these elephant tusks, my illness will grow more severe each day!
The King, having always held him in high esteem, did not dare to refuse his wish; he immediately summoned several hundred hunters from within the kingdom and addressed them, saying:
"Have you ever seen in the mountains a white elephant with six tusks?"
They all replied,
"We have never seen such a thing.
The king was displeased.
The lady summoned the hunters and spoke to them of this matter.
She said, "There are truly no such elephants in the vicinity here; among you, who is there one capable of enduring hardship and possessed of great courage?"
A certain man knelt for a long time and said,
"I am the most worthy! Thereupon,
the lady gave him ten thousand taels of gold, along with an iron hook, an axe, a chisel, and a set of Dharma robes, and addressed him:

“You shall go directly into the Snowy Mountains; along the way there will be a great tree with pythons on both sides, each several hundred *zhang* in length and impossible to approach. You must pass through the center by boring into the tree with an axe and chisel.”

On the way ahead, one will see a great body of water with trees growing along its edge; taking an iron hook, one should hook onto a tree branch and advance by following the branches until reaching the place where the elephant resides.
Observe a place where the elephant usually stops; immediately dig a deep pit there and cover it thinly over the top. While waiting for the elephant to come by, shoot it with an arrow from within.
He immediately donned the *kāṣāya* robe according to the dharma of a śramaṇa and said, "The elephant honors the Triple Gem; he will never harm you.

Following these instructions, the hunter set out on his way. On the seventh day of the seventh month of the seventh year, he arrived at the place where the elephant resided, dug a pit, and entered it.

In a short while, the elephant king returned; the hunter struck him with a poisoned arrow. Wounded by this shaft, the elephant did not come from afar but immediately used his trunk to clear the surrounding ground. Seeing a person in a pit, he asked: "Who are you?"
The man, seized with great fear, confessed, saying, "I am the person who responded to the call.
The Elephant King immediately realized it was the work of the lady; he then broke off his own tusks and gave them to the hunter.
He said to the man:
"Go back; as soon as the elephants see you, they will surely harm you. I have instructed them to retreat, but the herd will surely follow your tracks to pursue you."
Protected by the majestic spiritual power of the Elephant King, she emerged from the border region within seven days and returned to her own country, where she gave the elephant tusks to the Queen.
Upon receiving them, the Queen examined them repeatedly; she was both filled with joy and remorse, and before long, she died from vomiting blood.

When Śākyamuni Buddha was in the world, he was preaching the Dharma at a great assembly of devas, nāgas, spirits, and the four classes of disciples. Among those seated in the assembly was a great bhikṣuṇī who, gazing afar at the Buddha, let out a loud laugh; a moment later, she raised her voice and wept. Among those seated in the assembly, there was no one who did not find this strange.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"How is it that this bhikṣuṇī has attained arhatship, yet for what reason is she so overcome with both grief and joy that she cannot control herself?
I wish to hear the account of these matters."

The Buddha told Ānanda: "At that time, the White Elephant King was my own self; the Queen was the present Gopī; and the junior queen was this present bhikṣuṇī. Because she had attained supernatural powers (abhijñā) and recognized her past lives, she wept because she did not serve those whom her heart loved. She laughed because those who sought to harm virtuous people instead attained the Way through her."
When the assembly heard this, they all thought to themselves:
"If even those who have created evil karmic conditions with the World-Honored One can still attain deliverance, how much more so for those who possess the karmic conditions of virtue and the Way!"
The entire assembly conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, vowing to extensively deliver all beings throughout the ten directions.

(10) Formerly, when the Buddha went to the kingdom of Nagna at the invitation of Sujāta, that country was near the sea. As the dragon raised clouds and rain, the Buddha feared the people would be swept away; having accepted the food and drink, he led the multitude to Lake Anavatapta.
When the Buddha’s assembly had concluded and the multitude were seated, he announced,
"Śāriputra is not present among the assembly.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, thought to himself:
“The Buddha’s left and right sides are always graced by those with supernormal powers and wisdom, who further enhance the Buddha’s radiance.
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, addressed Maudgalyāyana:
“Go and summon Śāriputra here.”
Maudgalyāyana paid his respects and departed.
Śāriputra was mending his Dharma robes when Maudgalyāyana said, "The Buddha is at the great assembly of the gods by Lake Anavatapta; the Buddha has sent me to summon you, so please go at once."
Śāriputra said, "Wait until my robe is finished.
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"If you do not leave at once, I shall, by means of my supernormal power, take you, this mountain, and the stone chamber and place them in my right palm, then carry you to the Buddha’s dwelling.
Śāriputra then untied his waistband and placed it on the ground,
saying to Maudgalyāyana, "If you can cause this waistband to leave the ground, then my body may be lifted."
Maudgalyāyana immediately tried to lift it, causing the earth to tremble, yet he could not raise the girdle.

Maudgalyāyana returned to the Buddha’s presence by means of his supernormal power; Śāriputra was already seated by the Buddha’s side, and Maudgalyāyana thereby realized that the power of supernormal faculties is inferior to the power of wisdom.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu among those seated whose ear was adorned with a sumana flower. The entire assembly was filled with doubt, wondering:
"The dharma of a bhikṣu requires detachment from floral ornaments; why then does this bhikṣu wear a flower?"
The Heavenly Lord immediately addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I do not understand why this bhikṣu wears flowers.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Remove the flowers from within your ears.
The bhikṣu followed the instruction and immediately pulled the flowers away with his hand;
yet they continued to appear as before, and though he removed them again and again, they remained in their original place.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu,
"Remove it by means of your supernormal power (ṛddhi).
He then, through the power of samādhi, manifested tens of millions of hands and plucked the flowers from his ears in mid-air, yet the flowers were not exhausted.
The assembly then realized that this was due to the causes and conditions of their past virtue, and was not merely a fleeting manifestation of flowers.
The Heavenly Emperor addressed the Buddha:
"I pray that you will explain the beginning and the end of this matter, so that the doubts of those gathered here may be resolved."
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:
"In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, the Buddha was holding a great assembly to preach the Dharma.

At that time, there was a drunken guest in the assembly listening to the teachings; hearing the sutra, he rejoiced, placed flowers upon his ears, took them and scattered them over the Buddha, prostrated himself, and departed."
After his life ended, he received blessings among devas and humans for ninety-one kalpas and never again entered the three evil realms.

If you wish to know who that person was at that time, it is this very bhikṣu here; because he scattered a single flower, the merit has continued until he attained the Way, and thus it remains inexhaustible.
The Heavenly Emperor addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In the past, there was a drunken guest who neither received the precepts nor practiced the six pāramitās; yet the merit from that single scattering of flowers has not been exhausted until now after ninety-one kalpas, let alone for those who performed it many times!"
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:
"You should know that the benefit of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) for all beings is just like this.
When the entire assembly heard this teaching, they were filled with great joy and universally resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

11 (11). Once, when the Buddha had first attained the Way, there was no one in the world whom he did not convert through his teaching; yet the King of Śrāvastī alone did not believe or understand at that time.

The Buddha’s vihāra and the royal garden pavilion were adjacent to one another, both bordering the river; within the vihāra there were more than three hundred śrāmaṇeras, each assigned to serve the Three Honored Ones.
At that time, the *karmadāna* sent several novices to fetch water from the river, each carrying a jar.
When the novices reached the riverbank, they took off their *kāṣāyas* and played at building huts.
At that time, King Prasenajit’s queen was sitting atop a multi-storied pavilion; seeing from afar how the śrāmaṇeras were playing together in such a manner, she said to the king:
"My lack of faith in Gautama is indeed justified by this."

"Gautama and his followers claim for themselves that they are pure and free from the hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), yet their current indulgence in play and pleasure is no different from ours; how can they be said to be true?
The lady replied to the king:
"For example, as with the dragons and serpents in the ocean, so too is the Mahāyāna Dharma!"
"There are those who have attained the Way and those who have not yet attained it; they cannot be discussed as one and the same!

Before the lady had finished speaking, the śrāmaṇeras donned their robes, each took water, and set out directly for the location of the vihāra. Using their supernormal powers, they lifted three hundred jars into the air and flew after one another, all entering the vihāra.
The lady then pointed out what the Great King had said:
"If Your Majesty’s intention was not yet fulfilled, how about manifesting your supernormal powers now!

Upon seeing this, the King was filled with great joy; he immediately descended from his seat and, together with his ministers and officials, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in worship, took refuge, and repented for his transgressions.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and the king, his consort, and the entire assembly all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
(12) Once, in the city of Śrāvastī, a brahmin and an elder went out of the city for recreation; traveling along, they arrived at the vicinity of the Jetavana.

The Buddha, knowing that this person possessed the merit to be delivered, immediately went forth and sat beneath a tree, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the realm of Jetavana; the trees, wood, earth, and stones all turned the color of gold.
Seeing the light, the brahmin asked his attendant,
"What kind of light is this?
The attendant replied:
“I do not know,” the elder said.
“Is it not the light of the sun?”
The people replied, "The sun is usually hot and scorching; this light is cool and temperate, so it cannot be the sun's light!
The elder asked again:
“Is there perhaps a firelight? The attendant replied, “This is not firelight;
fire flickers and is unstable, whereas this radiance is steady and constant—it does not resemble firelight!”
Having discerned this through reflection, he said to the elder,
"This is the light of the spiritual path of the śramaṇa Gautama!
The elder then replied:
"Do not say such things!
I do not like the Gautama; turn the chariot around quickly.

The Buddha then performed a miraculous transformation, so that on all three sides there spontaneously appeared great chasms through which one could not pass, except for a path directly in front of the Buddha.
A person came and said to him:
"The road passes by Gautama's side!
There is no other choice."
As before, seeing the Tathāgata from afar, she immediately covered her face with a fan;
the Buddha again employed his majestic spiritual power to make her see through both inside and out so that she could lift her eyes and thus meet the Buddha face-to-face.
Upon awakening, he descended from his carriage, prostrated himself, and paid homage.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, whereupon he immediately gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment and soon attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Even those who turn their backs on the Buddha can still attain the wisdom of the Way; how much more so, then, those who believe and incline toward him!
(13) Once, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there were eight great wrestlers, each possessing the strength of sixty elephants.

Among them was one man who alone possessed many extraordinary military tactics; he mastered the sixty-four transformations and was fully equipped in both civil and martial arts, relying on these to feel no fear or difficulty.
The Buddha perceived that this person was certain to fall into the evil realms, so he went to where he was in order to deliver him.
The gatekeeper reported:
"Gautama is outside, having come wishing to see you."
Upon hearing this, the Malla addressed those around him, saying:
"How could the wisdom of Gautama ever surpass mine?
He is not my equal!"
He said to the gatekeeper, "Send him away; I cannot see him!
Thus, the Buddha went to the gate three times and was not seen.
Thereupon, the Buddha manifested as a young strongman to lean against the gatepost. When the gatekeeper entered to report this, the strongman asked, "Could these be the eight men of this kingdom?"
The gatekeeper replied:
"He is merely a youth!
We have never seen him before!"
The wrestlers went outside to meet him and led him to the arena; disregarding his youth, they wished to strike him down and said to the youth, "Come forward boldly, let us wrestle together."

The two men stepped forward together, and as they were about to join him, the Buddha used his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to lift them into the air at a height of more than ten *zhang* above the ground. Looking down toward the earth, they saw only blades of fire; their arrogance and anger completely vanished, and fearing death, they cried out from mid-air, "We take refuge in the One Below."
The strongman obtained his life intact; when he looked back at the ground, he saw the Buddha's body.
Realizing it was the Buddha, the strongman prostrated himself in homage and said:
"I now know that the Buddha’s power of spiritual footprints (*ṛddhi-pāda*) is such as this; henceforth, I shall never again dare to be arrogant."
"I pray that you will grant me forgiveness so that my heavy calamity may be extinguished.
The Buddha immediately accepted his plea and expounded the profound Dharma for him.
He then gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment, and immediately attained the stage of *avaivartika*.
Such is the extent of what is delivered by the Buddha’s skillful means.
(14) Once, in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, there was the son of a brāhmaṇa who lived alone with his mother. When he had grown up as a youth, he asked his mother, "What did my father serve and worship?"
"I wish to follow his tracks.
The mother said to her son,
"When your father was alive, he would enter the water to bathe himself three times every day."
The son said, "Father, having done this, what do you hope for?
The mother said:
“The Ganges Water can remove defilements and enable one to attain supernatural powers!
The son replied, “Not so.”
The mother said to her son,
"Do you perhaps have some different view?
The son replied:
"If that were so, why do the inhabitants on the north bank of the river—who daily drive their oxen south across it and bathe twice a day—not attain the Way?
Furthermore, there are fish, turtles, and other such creatures in the water living there; why do they also not attain the Way?"
The mother asked,
"What do you think? The son replied:
"Only the water of samādhi from the Tathāgata’s pool of the eight liberations can wash away these defilements; only then will one attain the unconditioned.
Thus he replied to his mother, saying that they should go to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek purification through his divine transformation.

Thereupon, mother and son went to where the Buddha was. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them; the son became a śramaṇa and attained the path of arhatship. He then returned to preach the Dharma for his mother, who in turn attained the path of srotāpanna.
*Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume I;
*Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume II.
Translator unknown; appended to the Later Han Records.
15. (Fifteen) Once, in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there was a bhikṣu who extensively instructed several hundred disciples.
Among them were those who had attained the four dhyānas, those who had attained the five supernormal powers, those who had attained the stage of srotāpanna, and those who had attained arhatship.
At that time, an Anxi man arrived in the kingdom of Kaśmīra; seeing how the bhikṣus were thus teaching and transforming others, he conceived a heart of faith and joy and became their disciple.
Before long, he attained the five supernormal powers and manifested his miraculous feats before the multitude.
The Master told him:
"Although you have attained the five supernatural powers, your mental fetters are not yet resolved; do not manifest your spiritual feats to become conceited!
The disciple then became resentful toward his teacher, thinking that the teacher was jealous of his excellence, and he said to himself:
"I shall return to my native land to manifest my spiritual power!
He then flew to his home country and appeared before the palace of the King of Anxi, manifesting his supernormal powers as he arrived by flight.
The king paid him homage and asked,
"Of what country is this practitioner?
The bhikṣu replied:

"The king and the people of my country went to the kingdom of Kaśmīra to study the Way. Now I have returned because I wish to bring blessings to this land and repay the kindness of those who gave me birth.
The king was greatly delighted and immediately knelt down, saying:
"I pray that you, O Master, will reside in my palace from this day forward and accept my offerings."

The bhikṣu consented. The king personally provided offerings with his own hands, or sent his queen and court ladies to do so; however, the bhikṣu then developed lustful intentions toward a maidservant. When the ministers and subordinates learned of this, they informed the king, who rebuked him.
The reason the king did not believe [the bhikṣu’s earlier claims] was that he had originally seen him fly there.

Before long, her lower garment became swollen with pregnancy. The ministers reported this again to the king; taking his wife as evidence, he realized the truth of the matter. He immediately confiscated her religious robes and dispatched a messenger to send her out of the palace. Because she was a practitioner of the Way, he did not subject her to torture or cruel punishment.
A bhikṣu went abroad to commit robbery and plunder; as there was no one before him to oppose him, the king did not know that he was the bhikṣu who had previously been there, and said:
"Recruit brave men to capture him alive."
When he was brought forward, it was clearly the former bhikṣu;
the king asked him, "Previously you committed lust, claiming it was merely a mistake; why do you now rob people?"
The bhikṣu bowed his head and said, "I am destitute; I have no other recourse!
The king said:
"I originally saw that you were flying here by means of your supernormal power; therefore, I could not bear to inflict harm upon you.
I further grant you amnesty: do not again trespass within my domain.
Having said this, he released him and let him go.
The bhikṣu thought to himself,
"It is like a traveler working for hire to seek a livelihood!
and immediately began to advertise himself.

There was a butcher who hired him to beat oxen and stab sheep; he performed every task for him. Later, when ordered to break bones, a splinter flew up and struck his face, destroying his visual faculty so that he could no longer see. No longer fit for service, the master sent him away.
Thereupon, carrying a broken bowl, he went from street to street begging for alms and thus became a lowly person.

After the bhikṣu had undergone this transformation for several years, his teacher observed him with his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), wishing to know his whereabouts; he saw that the bhikṣu was thus begging in the marketplace of An-hsi.

At that time, among his disciples were more than five hundred who studied only the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and did not seek the cessation of suffering. The Master addressed them, saying:
"Prepare yourselves quickly; we shall now go together to visit the disciples of our former master, An Shigao."
The disciples were all delighted and said, "His virtue and Way must surely be most flourishing.
The Master then personally humbled himself to go and visit them; by means of his supernatural power, he arrived in an instant and stood before them.
The Master called his name by its sound, and he immediately replied to the Master’s voice,
saying, “Has the Master come? The Master said:
"Therefore, I have come to visit you.
The Master asked,
"For what reason is this so?"
The disciple related the beginning and end of the matter in detail, explaining the intent behind his transgression.
The master said to his disciples:
"Attaining the five supernormal powers is not the firm and stable path; it is not something to be relied upon!"

When the Master spoke these words, five hundred disciples all attained the six supernormal powers and realized the path of Arhatship. That one disciple was filled with shame and had no words to say; the teacher and his entire retinue then returned together to their original dwelling place.
16. (16) Once there was a kingdom that was prosperous, abundant, and densely populated. When another country desired to seize it, they immediately mobilized their army and marched forth.
The people within the kingdom, having become aware of this, raised a great army; everyone from those aged fifteen upwards to those under sixty was required to go on campaign.

At that time, there was a man who wove cotton cloth; he was approaching sixty years of age. His wife was upright and virtuous, yet she habitually treated her husband with contempt. The husband, however, always respected his wife as a superior person and served her.
The husband said to his wife: "We must now depart; we have been commanded to prepare our own weapons, provisions, and utensils."
"I pray that you will grant me leave at this time.
The wife gave her husband a five-sheng vessel for storing grain, and a shuttle for weaving cotton cloth made of wood, one zhang and one chi in length.
The wife said:

"You have brought this conduct into our quarrel; there is nothing else [to be gained]. Even if you were to break this vessel or lose these hemp-wood goods, we shall no longer live as householders with you."
The husband then took his leave, not thinking that he might be harmed by the army, but fearing only that the two items might be misplaced and cause him to lose his wife!

On the road he encountered those soldiers and fought with them; when the army was defeated and retreated, he realized that if the two items on the cotton cloth were misplaced, he would lose his wife’s favor. As everyone fled, he took up the shuttle, placed it upon his head, and stood alone facing the enemy.
When the enemy army saw this, they cried out,
"A hero! and did not dare advance further, but retreated instead.
Thereupon, the king's army was able to reorganize its ranks; by advancing with united strength in battle, they achieved a great victory.
The enemy forces were no match for them, and their dead and scattered remnants were nearly exhausted.
The king was greatly delighted and prepared to reward those who had performed meritorious service, whereupon the people addressed the king:
"The cotton-weaver should be granted the highest reward.
The King then summoned him to see him and asked the reason for his intention:
"By what means were you alone able to repel the great army?"
He replied, "I am certainly not a warrior.

My wife provided me with two items for my military service; had I lost these two items, she would have abandoned me and failed to maintain our household. Therefore, I risked death to complete these two items so that I might repel the enemy army; it was truly not due to any prowess or strength!"
The king said to his ministers:

"Although this man was originally afraid of his wife, he has nonetheless saved the state from calamity; he shall be granted the highest merit. He was immediately appointed as a minister, and bestowed upon him precious goods, houses, and palace ladies. His status was second only to the king's, and his descendants inherited these blessings, succeeding one another for generations.
This worldly phenomenon is obtained through causes and conditions.

The Buddha borrowed it as a metaphor: the wife, the husband, the five-sheng vessel, and the one-chi-long wooden beam represent the Buddha bestowing the Five Precepts and the Ten Wholesome Actions upon his disciples!

The Master said: "Those who firmly maintain these two things without letting them be destroyed or lost may dwell with me; this means that those who uphold the Dharma and do not transgress it even unto death shall ascend together with the Buddha to the Hall of the Way."

That one shall both defeat the enemy's army and receive honors and rewards is like a person who observes the precepts: in this present life, adversaries are suddenly confronted and utterly extinguished, while in future lives, blessings and the heavenly realms are naturally attained!

17 (17) Once, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a wealthy and noble brahmin who possessed immeasurable riches and was endowed with keen intelligence and clear wisdom; yet he had fallen into wrong views and did not believe in the wholesome, saying:
"It is useless!"

At that time, Śāriputra perceived this with his divine eye and thought: "This elder possesses great merit from past lives and has attained such wealth and status; yet because of his attachment to food, he will surely fall back into the three miserable realms without creating new merit. I must go to deliver him."
He then manifested his supernormal power and stood before him holding an alms bowl.

At that time, as the Brahmin was sitting down to eat, he saw Śāriputra and became extremely enraged; he immediately pushed him out of the house, struck him with his hands, and then returned to sit and eat. He neither invited him to sit nor sent him away. When he had finished eating, washed his hands, and rinsed his mouth, he took a mouthful of water and spat it into Śāriputra’s bowl, saying:
"Take this and go; I give this to you as a gift."
Śāriputra said, "May you receive immeasurable blessings throughout the long night. Having said this,
he immediately departed.
The elder was terrified and feared that [Śāriputra] would go and report his words, so he sent men to track him down.
Śāriputra had already returned directly to the vihāra; he mixed water with mud and plastered the place where the Buddha used to walk. He addressed the Buddha, saying:

"That man was stingy and greedy, yet when given a single mouthful of water, he now uses it to plaster the place where the Buddha walks. I pray that the Buddha will walk upon it, so that he may receive immeasurable merit throughout the long night."
The Buddha immediately entered the *caṅkrama-samādhi* (the meditative absorption of walking meditation).
The attendant sent by the elder witnessed all of this and returned to report to the elder:
"The Buddha has renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King to become a śramaṇa; he carries his almsbowl to seek food, yet he has no craving or seeking!"
"It is only because I wish to deliver sentient beings!
He explained the matter from beginning to end.
The elder felt great remorse for his lack of devotion, and the entire family, both old and young, went together to the Buddha's dwelling to repent and apologize for their transgressions.
"I am foolish and have acted recklessly; I pray you will forgive my grave transgression.
The Buddha accepted his refuge and preached the Dharma for him; his doubts were resolved, his fetters were severed, and he attained the stage of non-retrogression.

18 (18) In the past, the kingdom of Pāriyātra was more prosperous and flourishing than any other country. It was fully endowed with the nine grades of beings, from the True Persons and divine beings down to the unworthy; it likewise possessed both the scriptures of the immortals and secular texts. Gold, silver, grain, and silk—there was no commodity that was not present there. Consequently, the Buddha often referred to it as the "Country of Renowned Things."
At that time, the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist sectarians all deliberated together, saying:

"The Buddha says that there is nothing in this land that does not exist; we should go together to seek out what this land lacks, and by means of this, refute him so that he no longer remains sincere. Only then shall we surely receive his respectful service."
The brahmins deliberated, saying:

"We have never heard of rākṣasa demons existing in this kingdom; we must have sought them in vain, for they could not possibly be found. This clearly shows that the Buddha’s realization of the Way is not correct!"
He wandered through the market streets searching everywhere for one he wished to buy as a ghost, but found none.
The Brahmin was delighted and said, "I have devised a clever stratagem.
Knowing the Brahmin’s secret scheme, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately descended and transformed himself into a merchant, sitting in a stall as if selling goods.
The brahmin walked through the marketplace in succession until he came before him and asked,
"Do you have any ghosts for sale?
The Heavenly Emperor replied:
“There are some; how many heads do you wish to have?
The brahmins said to one another, “This is mere empty talk! From whom could he obtain ghosts to sell, that he speaks of ‘how many heads’?”
The brahmins said, "We wish to obtain several heads.

Then the Lord of Devas opened the shop door, and suddenly there were several dozen demonic heads. Seeing this, the brahmins were struck with great terror; yet each, reflecting in his heart, recognized the Buddha’s utmost sincerity, and they all approached the Buddha to take refuge, saying:

"Although the kingdom of Pāri possesses all manner of things, one who goes there empty-handed will not obtain a single item; yet if one brings wealth and goods to buy, there is nothing that cannot be obtained.

Taking this as a metaphor, it illustrates what is seen in the world: it is like the city of Sarvajñatā (All-Knowledge), wherein there is nothing that does not exist—the four immeasurables, the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, from the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas up to the Tathāgata. If there is a person who does not cultivate virtuous conduct, yet hopes to obtain something within Sarvajñatā, it cannot be attained!
If one reveres the holy teachings and restrains body, speech, and mind, it is like possessing goods: there is no wish that will not be fulfilled!
(19) Once, in the land of India, there was a Pine Monastery where four practitioners of the Way resided, all of whom possessed the six supernatural powers.
In the kingdom there were four lay devotees, each of whom invited a practitioner to provide him with long-term support.
These four practitioners each went forth to teach and transform others: one went to the abode of Śakra, Lord of the Devas;
another went to the abode of the Dragon King of the Ocean.
One person went to where the garuḍa was;
the other went to where the human king was.

Then, regarding the offerings received by these four practitioners of the Way, they divided the remains from their alms bowls and gave them to the donors to eat. These consisted of a hundred flavors, such as they had never seen before. Each asked the practitioners:
“From whom did you obtain this?
The practitioner then recounted the beginning and end of each of their stories for them.
Thereupon, the four laymen each made a vow.
One person said,
"I wish to be born in the palace of Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Another wished to be born in the ocean to become a nāga.
One person desired to be born among the Garuḍas;
another desired to be born as a son of a human king.
When their lifespans ended, they all attained rebirth as the Four Heavenly Kings.

At that time, they were mindful and desired to observe the eightfold fast; they searched throughout for a quiet place until they found only the secluded rear garden of the King of Magadha. They all entered the garden and sat beneath the trees, observing the fast with a compassionate heart and practicing the six recollections for one day and one night.
When the business was concluded the following morning, they approached one another and spoke;
the King of Magadha asked, "Who are you people? One man replied:
"I am a celestial king," said one. "I am a dragon king," said another.
One person said,
“I am the King of the Golden-Winged Birds.
Another person said:
"I am a king of men. Having thus understood the beginning and end of the matter, the four men were all greatly rejoiced.
The Heavenly King then said:
"We have all fasted together; who has obtained the greater merit?
The King said, "My desire was close outside the garden, yet the sound of the music reached here. To be able to concentrate my mind amidst this [distraction]—my merit is foremost."
The Heavenly King said:

"In my celestial realm, the palaces of the seven treasures, the jade maidens, the musicians, and food and clothing are all provided spontaneously; I have no further thoughts or desires. That you have come from afar to observe the complete fast is a response to merit that is foremost."
The Golden-Winged King said:

"That which I delight in is solely the eating of dragons, for it is more exquisite than the five kinds of music. Now that we dwell together in one place without even a hair’s breadth of ill will toward one another, my merit is supreme."

The Dragon King said, "Beings such as we are the provisions for the Golden-Winged Bird; we are constantly terrified of being eaten and hide ourselves in concealment. Now, while staying in one place, we have divided our deaths to maintain complete purity of observance, and thus my merit is supreme."
The King of Magadha said, "I have a wise minister named Piyaka; I shall invite him to resolve this matter.

He immediately summoned him, and upon his arrival, he explained his intention in detail. Piyaka then took four kinds of silk—blue, yellow, white, and black—and suspended them in the air, asking the Four Kings:
"Do these four colors exist within space, each distinct from the others?
The Four Kings replied,
"The distinctness of the colors is evident!"
The minister asked,
"Is it not strange that a shadow of a silk cloth appears upon the ground? He replied:
"It is not different!
The minister said:

"Now, the four types of embodied existence are each distinct, just as the substance of various silks and dyes differs; yet the present Dharma-fasting has a single flavor in its aspiration, just as the shadow cast by the earth is uniform without variation."

"Now these four honored kings have resolved their minds upon the Great Way, practicing diligence, compassion, and the fast; when they attain Buddhahood, their marks shall likewise be uniform, without any difference.
The four kings rejoiced and immediately attained the eye of the Way.
20 (20) Once, there was a householder named Pukāra who had two sons. When his father fell ill and was nearing death, he entrusted the younger son to the elder, saying:
"Your younger brother is young and knows nothing yet; I now entrust him to you. Take good care of him and provide for him well, so that he does not suffer from hunger or cold."
The father and son parted in grief and were lost to one another thereupon.
Later, the wife said to her husband:
"Your younger brother will soon grow up and trouble our household; all our possessions shall be divided between you. Since he is not yet grown, why do you not send him away?"
At first the elder brother was unwilling, but after the younger brother spoke repeatedly and would not stop, he finally complied.
He led his younger brother out of the city to a deep grave, bound him to a cypress tree, and—unable to kill him with his own hands—intended to let tigers, wolves, and evil spirits devour him.
He said to his younger brother, "You have repeatedly offended me; let you stay here overnight to reflect upon your transgression, and tomorrow I shall welcome you back.
Having said this, he abandoned him and departed.

In a short while, evening fell; owls, vultures, foxes, and wildcats were crying out everywhere. The younger brother was seized with great terror and had no one to whom he could turn for refuge. He looked up to heaven and sighed, saying:
"Within the three realms, is there truly anyone compassionate and benevolent who will accept my surrender?"
"Today we are beset by calamity and harbor immeasurable fear.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata, beholding their plea for deliverance, sat upright in samādhi and emitted a great radiance called "Dispelling Darkness," which illuminated the cemetery; instantly, it became brilliantly bright.
Next, he emitted a ray of light called "Release from Bonds"; when the light reached the child, his bonds were immediately loosened and his body no longer suffered pain.
Next, he emitted a ray of light named "Satisfying All"; upon seeing this light, the child’s hunger vanished.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata followed the light to that place, personally untied the bonds with his own hands, and asked him:
"Where do you wish to go? The boy replied:
"May I become a Buddha and deliver all beings from their calamities, just as the Buddha does today.
Thereupon, he gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The Buddha then expounded for him various essential points of the Dharma, whereupon he attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti*).

He addressed the Buddha, saying, "Although my elder brother harbored evil thoughts and, violating filial piety, harmed me, it was because of this that he was able to see the Buddha and sever the suffering of birth and death; I wish to go and repay his kindness."
The Buddha said,
“Excellent! You should know that this is the time.”
He then flew by means of his supernormal power to his elder brother’s house.
When the elder brother’s wife saw him, she was filled with shame and fear, having no face to show, and immediately said to her husband:

"Although you used the words of your wicked wife to bind me and leave me at the cemetery, it is because of these very circumstances that I have attained the Way today; this is entirely due to your kindness!"
He preached the Dharma for his elder brother and sister-in-law, and they immediately attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
(21) Once, when the Buddha was among the Śakras, kings of the gods, they frequently descended to make offerings to the Triple Gem; yet Mahākāśyapa alone refused to accept them.
Why is this? It is because his original vow was solely to deliver those who are poor and destitute.
Thereupon, the Lord of Devas employed a skillful means, and together with his wife, he descended to become the husband and wife of a poor family, dwelling beneath a dilapidated thatched hut.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa entered the city to beg for alms. The Emperor’s father and mother came forward to greet him with prostrations and said, "We are cold and poor;
we pray you accept this coarse food."
Kāśyapa agreed. He turned Kāśyapa’s bowl upside down and filled it with ambrosia, making its appearance coarse and unattractive, though its substance possessed a hundred flavors.
When [the king] raised it, the fragrance and sweetness were extraordinary; he then entered samādhi and observed, realizing it was the Lord of Devas.
Kāśyapa said, "Your merit and fortune are so exceedingly lofty; for what reason do you not feel satisfied?
The Lord of Devas replied:
"The merit and retribution of the Triple Gem are exceedingly abundant and immeasurable; therefore, the wise are never satiated with them!
(22) (22) Formerly, there was a *pīṭhaka* monastery in a foreign land where more than a hundred monks constantly resided together to study.

There was a laywoman (*upāsikā*) who was diligent and well-versed in the scriptures; not far from the monastery, she provided daily meals for one śramaṇa. The community of monks themselves determined the order of precedence, beginning from the head of the list and proceeding to the end, after which they would start over again.
Whenever anyone went there, the upāsikā would invariably question them on the meaning of the sūtras; those who were modest about their own shallow learning often did not like to go.

There was a śramaṇa named Mahālu who had become a monk late in life and knew nothing at all. When his turn came to go for the meal, he walked very slowly along the path and failed to arrive at the appointed time.
An upāsikā encountered him and said, "This man is of advanced age and venerable; his gait is composed and dignified.
Thinking that he possessed great wisdom, she was filled with even greater joy and prepared fine food for him.
When the high seat had been prepared for him to preach the Dharma, the elder monk, who in truth knew nothing, spoke from his own experience, saying:
"It is truly a suffering for a person to be ignorant and without knowledge."
Upon hearing this, the upāsikā reflected:
"Ignorance, which knows nothing, is the very root of the twelve links of dependent origination.
It is because this cycle of birth and death is never severed that it leads to all manner of suffering and affliction; therefore, it is said to be 'extreme suffering.'"
Reflecting thus repeatedly, he immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna. He then rose and opened the storehouse, intending to take some cotton cloth to give as an offering to the practitioner;
however, the practitioner descended from his seat and departed, returning to the monastery.

The upāsikā went out, but she did not know where the man was; looking from within the gate, she could not see him either, and truly thought that he had attained the supernatural power of the Way and flown away.

The upāsikā then took a white cotton garment and went to the vihāra seeking the practitioner. Fearing he would be pursued and called back, the practitioner entered his room, closed the door, and hid himself. His teacher, having attained the six supernormal powers, saw that someone was pursuing him and concluded that he must have committed some offense.
He immediately entered meditative concentration and observed that the upāsikā had attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; he called Mahālu and ordered him to come out and receive the offerings.
The teacher explained the matter from beginning to end for him, and Mahālu rejoiced, also attaining the stage of *srotāpanna*.

23. (Twenty-three) Once there was an old woman who had only one son. When he fell ill and passed away, she carried his corpse to the cemetery and laid it down; overcome with grief, she could not bear her sorrow. She thought to herself:
"I have had only this one son to provide for my old age, yet he has abandoned me to die. What use is there in my living?"
He then ceased returning home altogether, intending instead to end his life in one place; he had gone without food for four or five days.
The Buddha, knowing this through his supernormal knowledge, went with five hundred bhikṣus to the cemetery.

The old woman saw the Buddha approaching from afar; his majestic spiritual light was radiant and brilliant. Awakened from her stupor as if waking from a drunken sleep, she went forward to the Buddha, paid homage, and then stood back.
The Buddha said to the woman, "Why are you here among the graves?"
He addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have but one son who has passed away, leaving me. My grief is so intense that I wish to die together with him in the same place.”
The Buddha asked the old woman,
"Do you wish for your son to live?
The mother rejoiced.
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"Bring me some auspicious incense and fire; I shall offer prayers so that you may be reborn.
He further addressed his aged mother:
"You should obtain the 'household fire' that does not lead to death."
Thereupon, the old woman went to seek fire; when she saw someone, she first asked:
"Has anyone in your household died, either before or after? He replied:
"They say that from their ancestors until now, all have died and passed away.

The responses of every household he questioned were exactly like this; having passed through dozens of houses without daring to take fire, he returned to where the Buddha was and said to him: "World-Honored One! [The people] say such things."
"One searches everywhere for fire, yet there is no household where one does not die; therefore, you have returned empty-handed.
The Buddha told the old woman:

"Since the beginning of heaven and earth, there has been no being that does not end its life. It is natural for the living to seek survival and it is likewise a cause for joy; why, Mother, are you so deluded as to search for death by following your son?"
Her mind was immediately awakened and enlightened, and she realized the principle of impermanence.
The Buddha then extensively expounded the essential teachings for her, and the old woman immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Among the countless thousands of people observing from the charnel ground, all conceived the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment.

24 (Twenty-four): In the past, the city of Rājagṛha was abundant with many people. The nine classes of society lived separately without intermingling. There was a distinct area of one hundred million *li*, and those who possessed a hundred million in wealth would enter therein.

At that time, there was a householder who intended to settle in that place; he engaged in business, toiling his body and restricting his expenditures while devising various schemes. Over the course of several decades, although he had accumulated ninety thousand units, he fell short of reaching ten million. He then fell gravely ill and knew for himself that he would not recover.
He had a son seven or eight years old, to whom he entrusted his wife, saying:

"My son is young; entrust him with my wealth and property so that he may extensively manage his livelihood until it reaches one hundred million. He must certainly reside within this [wealth], for only thus shall the wish for my survival be fulfilled!"
Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Once the funeral rites were completed, [the son] was brought in and shown his father’s treasures, [who said]:
"My father left this instruction for you: when you have grown up and possess one hundred thousand, reaching a full one hundred million, and reside within a distance of one hundred million *li*."
The son replied to his mother, saying,
"Why must it be large?
You may give it to me now so that we may live together immediately."
The mother immediately gave it to him.
Thereupon, the youth used his wealth and precious treasures to make offerings to the Triple Gem and to bestow gifts upon the poor; within six months, his wealth was entirely exhausted.
The mother was filled with grief and distress, wondering at her son’s conduct.
Before long, the boy contracted a severe illness and subsequently passed away.
Having lost both her property and her young son, she was overcome with sorrow and constant remembrance of him.
Among them was one who was most wealthy; eighty people lived there, yet they had no offspring. Thereupon, the boy was reborn into that family as the son of the first wife.

When ten months had passed, he was born; he was handsome and intelligent, and naturally possessed the knowledge of his past lives. When his mother took him in her arms to nurse him, he resolutely refused to eat; it was the same when a maidservant took him to care for him.
When the stepmother heard that such a son had been born, she happened to go and see him.
Seeing him, she loved him; she immediately took him in her arms, cooed over him, opened her mouth, and asked for food.
The elder was greatly delighted and paid a heavy price to have her nurse and protect the child.
The elder then consulted with his wife, saying:

"My youngest son has a disposition such that when others hold him or try to feed him, he refuses to eat or drink; yet whenever this woman holds or picks up the child, he immediately becomes joyful. I now wish to go and fetch him to be my junior wife, so that she may raise and care for my son. Do you think this is acceptable?"
The lady listened to this and immediately sent a formal proposal to welcome him; she built a separate residence for him and provided him with a share of her wealth, leaving him in no want.
The son then said to his mother, "Do you know him?"
The mother, seized with great terror, said, "I do not know you.
The son said to his mother:

"I was formerly your son; having taken ninety millionth parts of your wealth to practice giving, we have now come together to become lords of eight billion [people], enjoying blessings without laboring. How wonderful this is!"
Upon hearing these words, his mother was both sorrowful and joyful.
When her son grew up, he transformed a hundred million *li* into the Mahāyāna path.
Therefore it is said:
"Even if one were to bring forth billions of them, a single village could serve as their dwelling; by establishing all beings in the gift of the Path, such is the entry of a Bodhisattva."

25 (Twenty-five): Once, in a foreign land, there was a man who cultivated many white cotton plants (*śāṭī*). If they were not harvested when the time had passed, their color would fade and they would become poor quality.

When the harvest time arrived, he hired many laborers at high wages; they worked day and night with little rest. Because his workers were so diligent and hard-pressed, the master prepared for them fine meat broth and excellent rice.

At that time, as the soup was about to be cooked, its fragrance wafted in all directions. An old vulture flew over it, and while clutching some excrement with its talons, it dropped it directly into the soup. When the cook saw this, he was about to scoop it out, but it had already completely dissolved away.
The cook thought to himself:
"If I wish to prepare more soup, the time is already late;
if I wish to take food and place it among the people, there will be impurity."
"Considering this small amount of excrement, it is not enough to spoil the flavor; it could be eaten by a person, but I simply would not eat it myself.

When the guests all came and sat down for their meal, the soup was served. The cook, being both a kitchen worker and hungry, ate the soup himself. Then the guest called out to the kitchen staff, saying, "Take some fine meat and eat it!"
The cook, knowing it to be impure and fearing he would lose the favor of others, forced himself to swallow it, yet he did not find it palatable.

The Buddha used this as a metaphor: sentient beings within the triple world, having escaped the desire for beautiful forms, fail to perceive their impurity and thus sink into delusion through successive rebirths. This is like a hungry man eating a delicious soup; the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the teaching of birth and death and manifests the reception of form, yet fully understands its impurity and finds no sweetness or pleasure in it—just as the cook was forced to eat the meat, swallowing it down without savoring its taste!

26 (26) Once, when Ānanda entered the city for alms, there was a girl from a family of sorcerers who had gone out to fetch water. Upon seeing Ānanda’s handsome appearance, she felt a desire toward him and returned to tell her mother:
"Outside there is a disciple of Gautama; bring him here for me."
The mother then summoned her spirit-medium, who deluded Ānanda so that he was unaware as he suddenly arrived at her house.
At that time, the mother of the sorcery said to Ānanda:
"I now offer my daughter to you; she may no longer leave."
Ānanda replied, "I did not follow her words.
The female sorceress then created a pit of fire and said to Ānanda:
"Would you rather be consumed by fire, or would you rather have my daughter?

Ānanda was struck with terror and focused his mind single-pointedly. The Buddha then extended his hand and stroked Ānanda’s head from afar. When the ghosts of the sorcerers saw the Buddha’s hand coming through the air, they were awed by its immeasurable majestic power and all fled in haste. They passed over and pushed the sorceress into the fire pit; her body was scorched and mangled, yet she was thus saved.
Ānanda immediately returned to the presence of the Buddha.
Later, the mother of the sorceress summoned the spirits and deities and rebuked them, saying:
"You were unable to turn Āgautama’s disciple and cause him to fall into delusion; for what reason did you push me into a fire pit?"
