The spirits and deities replied, "In the past, we joined with Pāpīyān and his eighty billion followers to go to the Pippala tree intending to destroy the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva pointed to the earth with his hand; that hand was slender and long, with webbed fingers, and its palm—both inside and out—bore the thousand-spoked wheel. His majestic spiritual power was immeasurable, and our eighty billion followers all fell prostrate, unable to regain their forms. Now he has extended his hand toward us again; we are truly cramped and terrified, which is why we flee in dispersal and ought not to remain."
"We spirits and deities follow our own constant customs; if one acts as a human being, we consider it a failure and intend to harm them ourselves.
We have long known this—what grounds are there to reproach us?
The mother of the sorceress then realized that the Buddha was the Honored One, immediately took the Three Refuges, and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
27 (Twenty-seven). Formerly, there was a grove of trees by the seashore, spanning several tens of *li*, where there were more than five hundred monkeys.
At that time, a mass of foam appeared upon the sea, hundreds of *zhang* in height and resembling the Snowy Mountains; it came with the tide and settled upon the shore.
When the monkeys saw this, they said to one another, "Is it not a joy for us to climb to the mountain peak and frolic about in the east and west?

At that time, one monkey climbed up and went straight down to submerge in the water. When the other monkeys saw this, they wondered why he had not emerged for so long; they thought he was finding such boundless pleasure within the foam-mountain that he did not wish to return.
They all vied with one another to leap into the mass of foam and drowned simultaneously.
The Buddha used this as a metaphor: "The sea refers to the sea of birth and death;

the mountain of foam refers to the body of the five aggregates (skandhas); the monkey refers to the human consciousness-spirit (vijñāna). Not knowing that the five aggregates are devoid of self-nature, they become attached through craving, desire, and delusion; thus they sink into the sea of birth and death with no prospect of escape."
Therefore, Vimalakīrti said: "This body is like a mass of foam; it is merely something to be washed and endured.

(28) Once, the elder Sudatta was seven times poor; later his poverty became most extreme until he had not a single coin left. Afterwards, he found a wooden measure in the midst of refuse; it was actually made of sandalwood. He took it to the market and sold it, obtaining four measures of rice. He said to his wife:
"I shall boil one peck of rice together; I will go to fetch some vegetables.
At that time, the Buddha thought to himself:
"I must deliver Sudatta so that his merit may be renewed."
Just as the rice was coming to a boil, Śāriputra arrived. Seeing him, the woman was filled with joy and placed the entire pot of one *drou* of cooked rice into his bowl.
When another *drou* of rice had finished cooking, Maudgalyāyana arrived; likewise, she joyfully gave it to him as well.
She again boiled another peck of rice, and when Kāśyapa went there once more, she gave it to him as well.
Just as the last peck was finished, she began boiling it again; then the Tathāgata himself arrived. The woman thought to herself:

"For several days we have lacked provisions and no one has come to us. Now that this rice is ready and the Tathāgata has come in person, could it be that my transgressions are coming to an end and merit is about to arise?"
He offered a bushel of cooked rice entirely to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha recited a mantra, saying:
"May your transgressions be extinguished and merit arise; from this day forth."
Sudatta soon returned home; his wife, fearing he might be angry, asked him:
"Now that the Buddha has come, and Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Kāśyapa have all arrived seeking food, shall we give them all the rice we have in the house?"
He replied, "I shall give it;
for a field of merit is difficult to encounter, and if someone comes to seek it, that is a fortunate meeting.
The wife said:
"Four pecks of rice! I have used it all!
The husband was greatly delighted, and the remaining rice gruel was drunk together by the husband and wife.

In a short while, as they wandered through the various rooms, precious jewels, food, grain, and bolts of silk spontaneously filled them to overflowing, just as they had been when they were wealthy in the past.

Sudatta leaped for joy, knowing that the Buddha had taken him into his compassionate care; he further invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha to provide offerings until the end of his life. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained the fruit of the Path (srotāpatti).
(29) Once there was the son of an elder who had recently welcomed a bride; they were deeply in love with and respectful toward one another.
The husband said to his wife, "Go into the kitchen and fetch some grape wine; let us drink it together.
The wife went to open the jar and saw her own reflection in it; thinking there was another woman there, she became greatly incensed.
She returned and said to her husband, "You already have a wife hidden inside a jar; why then did you come to take me?
The husband went into the kitchen himself to look, and upon opening the jar, he saw his own reflection. He became enraged at his wife, thinking she was hiding another man.
The two of them became increasingly enraged with one another, each calling the other's words true.
There was a brahmin who had long been on intimate terms with this son of a householder; encountering them as he went along, he saw the husband and wife quarreling and asked for the cause of it.
He went back to look at it again and saw his own reflection; filled with resentment toward the elder, he thought:
"While I have my own close kin hidden within the jar, you act as if we were fighting together?"
She then departed.
There was another bhikṣuṇī who had been supported by the householder; hearing of this dispute, she went to see it, but seeing a bhikṣuṇī inside the jar, she too became angry and left.
A moment later, another practitioner of the Way also went to look at it; realizing it was merely a shadow, he sighed deeply and said:
"The people of this world are foolish and deluded, taking what is empty to be real!"
He called his wife to enter together with him to look at it.
The practitioner said,
"I shall bring out the person from within the jar for you."
They took a large stone and smashed the jar; the wine was gone, and there was nothing left at all.
The two men’s minds were opened, and they realized it had been the shadow-form of the Buddha; each felt deep shame and remorse.
The Bhikṣu expounded for them the essential teachings of the Dharma, and the husband and wife together attained the stage of Avaivartika.
The Buddha used this as a metaphor:

"Those who see shadows fighting are like the people of the triple world who do not recognize the five aggregates, the four great elements, suffering, emptiness, or the three poisons of the body; thus, their cycle of birth and death does not cease."
When the Buddha spoke these words, countless thousands of people all attained the prediction of non-substantiality (*anātman*).
(30) During the time when the Buddha was in the world, there was a great wealthy family with six members to feed; their slaves, gold, silver, and precious treasures were beyond counting.
The Buddha and Ānanda were wandering for alms through the streets when they passed the house of a former benefactor.
Upon arriving at the gate, the father, mother, son, wife, and grandchildren leaped for joy and invited the Buddha to enter and sit.
In his room there was only a woolen rug, yet the food vessels he offered as alms were all made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli.
Ānanda knelt down and addressed the Buddha:
"What fundamental merit did this man possess that led him to such great wealth?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"In a previous life, during a time of famine, this person’s family was so impoverished that when the grasses and trees withered from drought, they could only sustain their lives by going everywhere to gather water. Once, as they had prepared a soup and it was just finished cooking, a practitioner on alms-round appeared outside;
seeing the śramaṇa, his parents said: 'Give our portion to him.'"
The sons and grandsons each yielded their own portions to their parents to eat.

The six people simultaneously conceived this thought: that each would provide one day’s meal in turn, only regretting that there was nothing left in the household with which to offer it to the World-Honored One.

By virtue of this merit, they shall be born among gods and humans, always attaining peace, security, and abundant wealth. Because their resolve was equal, they have shared karmic conditions throughout successive lifetimes; now meeting once again, father, mother, son, and all others—great and small—simultaneously receive the five precepts. Upon the end of their lives, they will immediately be reborn in the heavens to enjoy immeasurable blessings.
31. Once upon a time, there were three men who were each equally poor, making their living solely by selling firewood.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, when the bhikṣus were bathing the image of the Buddha within the monastery, Śākyamuni Buddha was also present among them, serving as the *karmadāna*.
As the three men passed before the temple, they heard that the ritual bathing of the image was taking place that day, so they entered to see it.
Each of them made a vow together, placing a single coin before the image and each praying for their heart's desire.
One person said:
"May I have abundant wealth and treasures in future lives, and never again encounter such poverty; at the end of my life, may I be born into a great wealthy family.
May I have an only son who, upon reaching adulthood, becomes a disciple of the Buddha and is constantly reborn among gods and humans."
One person said:

"May I know how to act as a master physician, treating the illnesses of all people; may I obtain great wealth; and when my life ends, may I be reborn in the family of Jīvaka, becoming proficient in medical arts so that there is no illness I cannot cure, and furthermore, may I be reborn among gods and humans in constant, great prosperity and happiness."
One person said:
"May I have a long life in future generations and not suffer a short lifespan; may I be reborn in the twenty-four heavens above with a life span of sixty kalpas.
The Buddha said: "These three people each have a single vow; in every lifetime they shall obtain immeasurable merit. Now these three shall all become my disciples and attain the path of Arhatship."
32 (Thirty-two): There are seven perils for people of the world who enter the sea to gather treasures:
first, great winds arise simultaneously from all four directions, blowing the ship until it is overturned;
second, the ship is on the verge of breaking apart and leaking.
Third, when a person was about to fall into the water and die, they were able to reach the shore;
fourth, two dragons came ashore intending to devour him;
fifth, having reached level ground, three venomous snakes pursued him, intending to devour him.
Sixth, the ground is covered with hot sand; as one runs upon it, one's feet are scorched.
Seventh, looking upward, one sees nothing; the sun and moon are perpetually obscured, and one cannot discern the directions of east and west.
"It is exceedingly difficult.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"You all likewise possess these seven matters:"
First, great winds arise from the four directions, which refers to birth, old age, sickness, and death;
second, the objects received by the six sense faculties are limitless, analogous to a leaking ship;
third, falling into water and being on the verge of death, which refers to being seized by Māra.
Fourth, the two dragons coming ashore to devour [him] refers to the life-force being eclipsed by the sun and moon;
fifth, the three venomous snakes on level ground refers to the three poisons within the human body;
sixth, the hot sand peeling and rotting his feet refers to the fires within hell.
"Seventh, regarding 'looking upward and not seeing the sun or moon,' this refers to the place where one undergoes punishment—a realm of profound darkness with no prospect of escape.
The Buddha said to his disciples:
"You should take note of these words; do not associate with such people. By diligently practicing the six matters, one may attain liberation."
The Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables, Volume II.
